title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
summary: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $μ$s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

title: Empirical Brightening Model for Distant Long-Period Comets
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables. Accepted to PSJ
summary: Recent studies have shown the traditional comet brightening model, $Hn$, with a constant activity index $n$ (i.e., single slope in $\log_{10}(r_{\rm h})$), fails to accurately describe heliocentric lightcurves at large distances, where water-ice sublimation is inefficient. We present a new empirical model, $Hab$, for distant comet brightening in which the effective brightening slope varies with heliocentric distance, $r_{\rm h}$. Using a multi-year pre-perihelion dataset from uniform instrumentation for 23 comets, we found that $Hab$ provides the best match to long inbound arcs spanning a wide range in $r_{\rm h}$. The best-fit coefficients $a$ and $b$ cluster tightly for our best-observed comets, suggesting a common brightening behavior; we therefore also tested one- and two-parameter $Hab$ variants in which $a$ and/or $b$ are fixed to anchor values derived from these comets ($A_1 = 0.40 \pm 0.09$, $B_1 = -1.78 \pm 0.68$), either individually, jointly, or via a linear relation. The three-parameter $Hab$ model is strongly favored by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for the full lightcurve, justifying its added complexity for characterization. We also tested predictive performance against $Hn$. For brightness forecasting from limited initial data ($Δr_{\rm h} \lesssim 2.5$ au, the heliocentric distance range spanned by observations), $Hab$ itself predicts poorly, whereas a one-parameter reduction, with both coefficients fixed, predicts more reliably, including outperforming $Hn$ with a fixed $n \sim 2-4$. Two-parameter reductions with only one coefficient fixed typically reach predictions within 1 mag of the observed brightness after only $Δr_{\rm h} \sim 1.0$ au of inbound coverage.

title: Collisional Evolution around A-type Stars with Strong Silicate Features
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ), 17 pages, 5 figures
summary: Around luminous A-type stars, retaining micrometer-sized dust grains is difficult owing to the high radiation pressure that repels particles with sizes below the blowout limit. Yet such particles have been evidenced in the terrestrial zone around those stars, via pronounced silicate spectral features. An in situ planetesimal belt that collisionally replenishes the dust is expected to deplete quickly, limiting the lifetime of observable features. However, modeling of such systems often relies on a power-law description of the grain size distribution that has a lower size limit owing to blowout. Using more complex, collisional simulations instead, we investigated the temporal evolution of hypothetical planetesimal belts in the terrestrial zone around five A-type stars showing strong spectral silicate features. A collisional cascade that is modified by radiation pressure results in dust distributions that replicate observed spectral features without requiring other physical processes. While features can be altered by particles below the blowout limit, their magnitude is dominated by the emission of larger grains. Using the systems' ages, we investigated the origin of the planetesimal belt. For the three younger systems of our sample, a planetesimal belt that emerged from the protoplanetary disk phase can explain the observations. This is even possible for two older systems if the planetesimals are located at slightly larger distances than the dust, e.g., if the dust drifted inward owing to the Poynting-Robertson drag. Alternatively, a recent production of the planetesimals, for instance, in a giant collision event, could have happened only several million years ago.

title: Saturn's Formation at the Carbon Dioxide Iceline
comment: Accepted for publication in The Planetary Science Journal
summary: Saturn's bulk metallicity and atmospheric volatile enrichments exceed those of Jupiter. Combined with their similar heavy-element masses, this suggests that Saturn formed farther out in a protoplanetary disk whose metallicity increased with heliocentric distance. Numerous models argue that Jupiter formed near the H$_2$O iceline; Saturn's composition is therefore expected to reflect accretion beyond this region. We test whether Saturn's elemental enrichments can be reproduced by formation near the CO$_2$ or CO icelines using a one-dimensional viscous $α$-disk model that tracks the transport, sublimation, and recondensation of 13 volatile carriers. We compute time-dependent radial distributions of solids and vapors for $α= 5\times10^{-4}$--$5\times10^{-3}$ and varied CO/CO$_2$ abundance ratios, and compare the resulting metallicities and enrichments with Saturn's observed composition. Strong carbon and oxygen enrichment peaks result from the cold-finger effect, most prominently at the CO$_2$ iceline, where supersolar metallicities comparable to Saturn's envelope are achieved only for $α\le 10^{-3}$. Smaller C and O enrichment peaks also occur at the CO iceline, but the local protosolar nebula metallicity there never reaches Saturn's inferred value. At $\sim$0.2--0.3 Myr, carbon and phosphorus enrichments in this region match Saturn's atmospheric values, while noble-gas abundances remain near protosolar owing to their long diffusion times. These results identify material originating near the CO$_2$ iceline as the most likely source of Saturn's heavy-element inventory. For the conditions adopted in our model, our results imply that Saturn accreted this material early ($\lesssim0.3$ Myr), in a weakly turbulent disk ($α\lesssim10^{-3}$) with a CO$_2$-rich volatile inventory.

title: Spatial variability of CH4-to-CO conversion pathways in irradiated gas giant atmospheres: implications for chemical relaxation and 1D quench schemes
summary: Close-in gas giant atmospheres are in chemical disequilibrium. Solving 3D kinetics to capture one source of this disequilibrium, transport-induced quenching, is computationally demanding, so simplifications are used. General circulation models (GCMs) relax abundances on the timescale of a single conversion pathway. 1D models place a quench level and hold abundances vertically uniform above it. We test both simplifications on CH4 against aerosol-free, solar-composition GCM simulations with thermochemical kinetics for HAT-P-11b, HD 189733b, HD 209458b and WASP-17b. We find ten CH4-to-CO conversion pathways, varying with depth, longitude and planet. A single pathway controls CH4 quenching on the three cooler planets; on WASP-17b two compete. The CH4 quench level is 3D: where the atmosphere is hotter, or a faster pathway takes over, the conversion timescale shortens, the quench level rises and the quench-level abundance falls. On WASP-17b the pathway switch lifts the quench level over the substellar tropics, deepening equatorial CH4 depletion. A 1D quench treatment with the Zahnle & Marley timescale typically locates the quench level within a factor of two in pressure for CH4 and about four for CO on every planet. It fails above the quench level, where every quench scheme holds abundances vertically uniform. The minor carbon carrier, CH4 or CO depending on the planet, is wrong by up to two orders of magnitude, on HD 189733b in opposite directions at different latitudes. Quenching sets an abundance at the quench level but does not fix it thereafter; even without photochemistry, transport and conversion keep that abundance spatially structured.

title: The Fate of Ice Sheets on Near-Synchronously Rotating Land Planets
summary: Rocky exoplanets orbiting M dwarf stars are often assumed to be synchronously rotating, such that water-trapping in ice sheets on the permanent nightside may pose a threat to habitability. However, in compact M dwarf systems, gravitational interactions between planets may cause the substellar point to librate or circulate on millennial timescales and sporadically change direction or speed. Here, we use a 3D global climate model to quantify, for the first time, the water-trapping capabilities of these "near"-synchronously rotating exoplanets, with TRAPPIST-1e as our test case. Across a range of synodic day lengths, we find that there is a permanent polar ice reservoir and an increasingly large build-up of lower-latitude transient nightside ice for longer days. A persistent ice-free region develops on the dayside where surface conditions can sustain liquid water. However, this steady-state ice distribution may never be realized since the accumulation timescale may be slower than changes in the spin regime. Additionally, we revise the nightside ice build-up on a synchronously rotating exoplanet using a coupled atmosphere+ice numerical model that accounts for atmospheric lapse rate and isostatic adjustment feedbacks. We find that accounting for this ice-elevation feedback reduces the predicted ice accumulation by a factor of ~3. Taken together, our study suggests that water-trapping in ice sheets is less severe than previously thought for land planets orbiting M dwarf stars.

title: Planetesimal Delivery to Giant Planet Circumplanetary Disks: Bulk Ice Enrichment and an Ice-rich Iapetus
summary: The regular satellites of Jupiter and Saturn are substantially enriched in ice relative to the rock-rich solids of the outer Solar System. In addition, the satellites interior to Titan and distant Iapetus are icier than Titan itself. Collisional processes and subsequent migration can readily alter compositions deep in the planetary potential well, but producing a distant, ice-rich satellite with Iapetus's radius of about 700 km is a challenge \citep{mosqueira2026a}. We show that differential ablation and capture of icy and rocky fragments from differentiated outer Solar System bodies can explain the bulk Jovian and Kronian satellite ice enrichment and supply the substantial ice-rich inventory needed for Iapetus. For 1\,m--1\,km fragments with the canonical size-distribution index \(p=3.5\) and a source containing 30\% ice by mass, the fixed radial distance Saturn calculation deposits material with ice fractions of 0.66 (delivery of vapor-only rock) or 0.50 (with retained rock melt) at 20 Saturn radii and nearly pure ice at 60 Saturn radii. Following three-dimensional trajectories over repeated passages through the pressure-supported gas gives ice fractions of about 0.4 near 20 Saturn radii and 0.9 near 60 Saturn radii. The matching Jupiter calculation yields a similar bulk ice enrichment, with a corresponding compositional gradient across the Galilean satellite region. These delivery profiles supply ice-enriched material for satellite formation. Yet satellitesimal inward migration subsequently modifies the material incorporated into satellites and thus alters their bulk compositions. We briefly discuss the implications for the PDS~70 planetary system.

title: Post-fragmentation Morphological and Broadband Color Evolution of C/2025 K1 (ATLAS)
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to The Planetary Science Journal
summary: Comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) underwent major fragmentation after its 2025 October 8 perihelion passage at q ~ 0.33 au. We present four epochs of Johnson-Cousins BVR imaging obtained with the Mount Laguna Observatory 40-inch reflector on 2025 November 26, November 29, December 5, and December 8, sampling the subsequent evolution of the integrated fragment-coma complex. The images were homogenized to common circular two-dimensional effective point-spread functions before morphology was measured along the projected fragment axis. We evaluated 324 profile-extraction configurations and removed solutions whose localized peak landed on the search-window boundary. The fragment-axis surface-brightness enhancement relocates inward between November 26 and 29 and outward between December 5 and 8; the sign of both changes is recovered in every valid configuration and at all tested common target PSFs from 5.3 to 6.0 arcsec. Calibrated BVR photometry using Gaia DR3 synthetic Johnson-Kron-Cousins standards independently shows a repeatable November 26-29 change in broadband spectral shape: B-V decreases while V-R increases. The curvature index S'_(V-R) - S'_(B-V) changes by +3.47 (+1.50/-1.65) percent per 1000 Angstrom, with 99.1 percent of Monte Carlo realizations positive, while the full B-R reflectivity gradient remains approximately constant. Repeating the color comparison at a fixed projected radius of 2205 km produces nearly identical changes. The combined results are consistent with continued restructuring of the unresolved post-fragmentation inner coma, while broadband imaging alone cannot uniquely separate dust-color evolution, molecular emission, and changing contributions from unresolved fragments.

title: Partial Fragmentation of Comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS)
comment: To be published in the Astronomical Journal
summary: We present time-series observations of the long period comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) obtained in 2025-2026, bracketing the comet's fragmentation in early November 2025. We show that a simple radiation pressure model can explain many of the comet's properties: the rapid fading after fragmentation, the increasing mean particle size in the projected photometry aperture, and the time dependence of the surface brightness profile. Small dust particles ($\lesssim 100 μ$m) dominate the coma, with average dust velocity $\sim$ a few $\times$ 1 meter s$^{-1}$. The nucleus radius is estimated at $\sim$0.5 km and the dust properties are consistent with, but do not prove, an origin in nucleus rotational breakup, followed by being swept down the tail by radiation pressure.

title: The anomalously large transiting planet around Boyajian's star: evidence for a circumplanetary ring
summary: A recent study reported a transiting giant-planet candidate with a mass of $9.4^{+4.9}_{-4.1}\,M_{\rm J}$ and a radius of $1.7\pm0.1\,R_{\rm J}$ on a wide orbit around Boyajian's star (KIC 8462852, also called Tabby's star), which is well known for its irregular, deep flux dips. The reported radius is puzzling, because cool giant planets of $\sim$10\,$M_{\rm Jup}$ are expected to have radii close to Jupiter's, so the companion appears $\sim$60--70\% larger than standard models allow. Here we explore the solution that the planet is actually ringed. We develop a fast and accurate code to compute the transit light curve due to a ringed planet, and apply it to the TESS light curve. The ring model is marginally favoured by the data by $Δχ^2>10$ and a difference in Bayesian information criterion (BIC) of $<2$. The preferred configuration is a Jupiter-sized ($1.1\,R_{\rm J}$) planet surrounded by an opaque, highly flattened ring extending to $3.1$--$4.4$ planetary radii with a nearly polar obliquity. While the ring geometry is uncertain, simple estimates suggest that a debris annulus extending out to the planet's Roche limit is needed to explain the large transit depth. The ring thus removes the radius anomaly altogether and is qualitatively consistent with the dusty, comet-shepherding environment inferred from the star's historic dimmings.

title: UV-driven organic precursor formation and dust evolution outside the snow line
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: In the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, dust grains are often mantled with a layer of ice containing simple molecules. The irradiation of the disk by far-ultraviolet (FUV) photons breaks such molecules, producing photoproducts (radicals, ions, and intermediary molecules) in the ice layer that can act as precursors to complex organics. As grains drift towards the warmer, inner region of the disk, their consequent sublimation of ices causes organic synthesis on their surfaces, potentially enhancing grain sticking and dust growth. In addition to interstellar medium radiation, FUV emission from the central star and nearby massive stars can contribute to photoproduct formation. We perform a vertical dust size evolution simulation including grain growth and fragmentation, and calculate photoproduct formation under irradiation from these three sources, treating the central star's FUV continuum and Lyman-$α$ emission separately. We find that enhanced UV irradiation, particularly from stellar Lyman-$α$ emission, significantly increases the total abundance of photoproducts formed. This results from both the strong stellar Lyman-$α$ flux and resonant scattering by the overlying hydrogen layer, which redistributes photons and directs a fraction toward the dust layer. Turbulent mixing and fragmentation cycles further redistribute grains vertically, allowing photoproducts to form throughout the disk. We find that stellar Lyman-$α$ irradiation can produce sufficient photoproducts to produce an organic mantle with an {organic-to-rock ratio of $\approx 10\%$}, which could enhance grain sticking. Our results suggest that FUV-driven organic synthesis may facilitate dust growth and contribute to overcoming barriers to planetesimal formation.

title: Mesoscale Modelling of Titan's Shangri-La region: the impact of surface properties on winds
summary: The knowledge of Titan's near-surface atmosphere is sparse. The Huygens descent probe measured winds, and the multiple dune field observations and possible dust storms suggest active near-surface dynamics. The Dragonfly rotorcraft lander will fly close to the surface in the Shangri-La region, near the Huygens landing site, where complex dune orientations were observed. This study presents the first mesoscale modelling of the near-surface dynamics in this region. However, due to a lack of high-resolution topography data, synthetic maps of surface properties were built. The surface was divided into different topographical units, such as plains, mountains, etc. The slopes and height of those units were then parametrised. Maps of thermal inertia, albedo and the aerodynamic roughness height were also built. The mesoscale model is coupled to a comprehensive radiative transfer code and forced by a global climate model. No moist processes are considered in this study. Topography has a major impact on near-surface wind amplitude and direction through slope flows and valley circulations. The majority of the winds are below 0.25 m/s. These winds induce a sensible heat flux comparable to the surface solar flux. Spatially varying thermal inertia has the biggest impact on the wind and surface temperature, with high values leading to smaller diurnal amplitude. The seasonal variability is taken into account, with stronger winds in northern summer. Predicted mesoscale near-surface winds are capable of lifting dust over dune fields, with different orientations during the year, and can therefore potentially play a role in sediment transport on Titan.

title: A Warped Dust Ring in the CQ Tau Disk
comment: 20 pages, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The diversity of planetary orbital architectures calls for observational constraints on radial variations in disk-plane orientation, or warps, yet such variations in dust disks remain poorly characterized. CQ Tau is a promising target because its misaligned inner disk and candidate gas warp suggest a radially extended warp. We present the ALMA 1.3 mm dust continuum image reconstructed from the real part of the visibilities, extracting the centro-symmetric disk structure. At an effective spatial resolution of $0.052'' \times 0.042''$ ($7.8 \times 6.3$ au), the image reveals a bright main ring at radii of $\sim20$--$70$ au and an unresolved compact emission component tracing the inner disk around the central star. Ellipse fits centered on the stellar position to contours tracing the inner and outer edges of the ring reveal radial variations in position angles and inclinations. At the inner edge ($\sim21$--$26$ au), the position angle and inclination span $214^\circ$--$233^\circ$ and $23^\circ$--$39^\circ$, respectively, while they span $231^\circ$--$235^\circ$ and $33^\circ$--$36^\circ$ at the outer edge ($\sim58$--$67$ au). Whereas a coplanar ring toy model fails to reproduce such variations, a warped ring model with the local tilt decreasing from $\sim4^\circ$ at $r = 20$ au to $\sim1^\circ$ at 60 au reproduces them. The high-pass-filtered real-part image reveals a pair of opposed curved negative residuals. Similar features appear only in the warped ring model, further supporting the dust warp. These results establish CQ Tau as an example of a warped dust disk and an important laboratory for investigating the connection between three-dimensional disk geometry and planet formation.

title: Post-DART impact ejecta re-accumulation on Dimorphos and implications for Hera gravity measurements
summary:
Context. The DART impact might have substantially modified the surface and near-surface structure of Dimorphos, affecting the morphology and gravity field that is to be measured by ESA's Hera mission.
  Aims. We investigate the post-impact redistribution of ejecta and its dependence on the assumed internal structure of Dimorphos.
  Methods. We performed high-resolution SPH simulations of the DART impact into two low-cohesion rubble-pile models, with and without a large central boulder. We followed the processes of ejecta re-accumulation and gravity evolution for six hours.
  Results. The impact ejects about 13% of Dimorphos's mass, most of which is re-accreted, producing near-global resurfacing. The ejecta blanket exceeds 8 m around the impact depression but is only a few tens of centimetres thick near the antipode, with similar large-scale deposition in both interior models. Local gravity changes reach about 10% of the pre-impact value. The central boulder affects the surface gravity only within the impact depression, where the removal of overlying material enhances its gravitational contribution.
  Conclusions. Hera will observe a surface and gravity field substantially modified by DART, which must be considered when interpreting measurements in terms of the internal structure of Dimorphos.

title: Spectroscopic Survey of Small Solar System Bodies with Ariel
comment: 16 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in RAS Techniques and Instruments (RASTI). Any comments are welcome
summary: The small Solar System bodies (SSSBs) preserve records of the formation and evolution of the Solar System. In particular, the near-infrared wavelength region around 3 $μ$m provides crucial insights into the origin and transport of hydrated materials and organics, although it is difficult to observe from the ground because of strong telluric absorption. We assess the observability of SSSBs as complementary science to the ESA Ariel space mission, operating in the visible to mid-infrared wavelength range (0.5--7.8 $μ$m). Using the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system, we evaluate the visibility of known SSSBs from 2032 to 2035. Our analysis shows that Ariel can spectroscopically characterize up to 402 unique SSSBs under a conservative limiting visual magnitude of $V=13.6$. If observations can be extended to somewhat fainter targets ($V=16$), the number of observable SSSBs could increase to 2144. Assuming operational scenarios in which one SSSB is observed every 3, 7, or 30 days over a four-year mission, the total numbers of observable targets would be 357, 209, and 49, respectively. We further model the spectral energy distributions of candidate targets to evaluate their observational performance. We demonstrate that Ariel can resolve critical absorption features, such as those at 2.7 $μ$m and 3.4 $μ$m, with a higher spectral resolution than the previous infrared survey with AKARI. Observations of SSSBs with Ariel can provide insights into the distribution and evolution of life-forming materials in the Solar System and constitute a scientifically compelling component of Ariel's complementary science program.
